newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Latam's oldest rebel army at "epicenter of poverty".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Latam's oldest rebel army at "epicenter of poverty".

text.p: A guerrilla column wades Indian-file through waist-high grass before melting away into the dense jungle backdrop.

A female rebel on lookout in an abandoned shack grips her Israeli-made Galil assault rifle in one hand and cradles a small green parakeet, her constant companion, in the other while scores of comrades file past, clad in olive-green fatigues and carrying high-powered weapons -- Galils, U.S.-made R-15s or the legendary Russian-built AK-47s.
This is Latin America's oldest and largest guerrilla force, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia-People's Army, known by its Spanish initials FARC.

"We all know we're going to die one day, we just don't know when. But it's better to die in the struggle than wait to be killed innocently," 22-year-old Patricia, another of the many young woman guerrillas, told Reuters at a sprawling FARC camp somewhere in the jungles of southern Caqueta province.

The camp, temporary home to some 500 rebels, was baptised simply as "Point X." The name is already being written into Colombian history books for the role it played in a process that political analysts believe could herald either the start of a process to end this Andean nation's three-decade-old internal conflict or the last stop before all-out war.

This was the final assembly point for 60 government soldiers taken prisoner by the FARC at the Las Delicias military base in neighbouring Putumayo province last Aug. 30. The troops were held for more than nine months before being freed in the town of Cartagena del Chaira on June 15.
ONE OF FARC'S GREATEST VICTORIES

A 5,000-square-mile (13,000 sq km) swathe of Caqueta's Caguan region was demilitarized to make way for the handover. Many analysts hail the Las Delicias attack and release process as one of the FARC's greatest politico-military victories since it was set up as a pro-Soviet guerrilla army in 1964.

Two days after the handover, the FARC's Southern Bloc, made up of more than 2,300 rebel fighters, invited Reuters into its camp -- the first time journalists have ventured into its headquarters since the bloc was set up in 1989.

Independent analysts believe the FARC may number as many as 18,000 fighters nationally and suggest the rebels are the de facto authorities in as much as 50 percent of the country where official state institutions are virtually non-existent.

Rebels, many the sons and daughters of humble peasant families, lounged under plastic sheets cleaning weapons and equipment. One typed the latest guerrilla communique on a laptop computer powered by a portable generator while others listened to radios or read political magazines.

All grumbled at the frequent media reports that portray the FARC as a rag-tag band of narco-terrorists more intent on running the local market in coca paste -- a raw material produced by dirt-poor peasants and used in the manufacture of cocaine -- than on the overthrow of the "bourgeois state."
THE EPICENTRE OF POVERTY

"The government has tried to portray this region as the epicentre of narcotrafficking ... but what we have around us is the epicentre of poverty," said the soft-spoken Comrade Fabian Ramirez, 31, head of the FARC's 14th Front and one of three Southern Bloc commanders.

As darkness fell more guerrillas trudged into camp, flashlights flickering like glow worms as they picked their way among the trees. In the distance a short-wave radio crackled, broadcasting messages to some of the 10 fronts that make up the Southern Bloc that were not present in the camp.

After a meal of lentils, rice and "agua panela," a warm sugary water, the insurgents retreat beneath their mosquito nets -- vital in the tropical rainy season. Shortly after daybreak the bloc will split up into its component units and the guerrillas will head into the countryside they know intimately, ready to continue their long war.

"I joined the FARC because I didn't see any way out apart from taking up the armed struggle," said William, 28. "If there was not a guerrilla, Colombia would be in even more of a mess now ... we want progress with social justice."

It takes about two years to turn raw recruits into full-fledged guerrilla fighters, able to care for their weapons, lay an ambush or discuss the ideological merits of Marx, Lenin or other revolutionary icons, Ramirez said. The maximum entry age is 30 and the minimum is 15, but it may be lowered for orphans or children of rebels killed in combat.

Community work in small villages dotted across the Caguan is also a key part of guerrilla training. In recent years rebels have helped the locals dig drains, pave roads and build a school and a house for teachers, Ramirez said.

Villagers in turn appear to treat the FARC as the primary political, economic and judicial authority in the zone and seek rebel leaders' advice on anything from raising funds for public works programmes to land disputes or even murder cases.
"It is not everyone who is capable of picking up a weapon but these lads (the guerrillas) are the response to social injustice. I love them," one local inhabitant said.
